title: "Vectorization"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

In this article, you will learn how to write a function for a single instance and apply it to a whole batch with `vectorize()`.

## What `vectorize()` Does

`vectorize(f)` returns a function that cuts its arguments into slices along an axis, applies `f` to every slice, as `lapply()` would, and stacks the results along an axis into one array.
By default, both are the last axis: the slices of a matrix are its columns, and the results of `f` become the columns of the output.

Below, `normalize()` scales a single vector to sum to one.
Vectorized, it normalizes every column of a matrix, which is what applying it to one column after the other and binding the results as columns gives:

```{r}
library(anvl)

normalize <- function(x) x / sum(x)
x <- nv_array(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2L), dtype = "f32")

vectorize(normalize)(x)

normalize_jit <- jit(normalize)
sapply(1:3, function(j) as_array(normalize_jit(x[, j])))
```

So a computation can be written for one instance -- one observation, one parameter vector, one sequence -- and applied to a whole batch.
Unlike that loop, and unlike `base::Vectorize()`, `vectorize()` does not call the function once per slice.
It traces the function once and turns every operation into one that works on the whole batch, so the result runs as a single program.
You can call the result of `vectorize()` directly, as above, or use it inside `jit()` to compose it with other operations.

## Choosing the Batch Axes with `in_axes`

By default, `vectorize()` maps over the last axis of every argument that is an array.
`in_axes` changes this.
A single axis applies to all of them, so for `f`, which computes the squared norm of a single vector, `in_axes = 1L` gives one norm per row instead of one per column:

```{r}
f <- function(x) sum(x^2)

jit(vectorize(f))(x)
jit(vectorize(f, in_axes = 1L))(x)
```

Negative axes count from the end, as elsewhere in anvl: the default is `in_axes = -1L`.
A named list gives each argument its own batch axis.
An argument that the list leaves out or gives `NULL` is passed to every application of `f` unchanged.
Here, every column of `x` is multiplied by the same weights `w`:

```{r}
g <- function(x, w) sum(x * w)
w <- nv_array(c(2, -1), dtype = "f32")

jit(vectorize(g, in_axes = list(x = -1L)))(x, w)
```

All arguments that are mapped over must have the same size along their batch axes.
Every array in a nested argument uses that argument's batch axis.

## Placing the Batch Axis with `out_axes`

The outputs are stacked along their last axis by default, `out_axes = -1L`, so a function that returns a vector returns a matrix with one column per slice.
`out_axes` puts the batch axis elsewhere.
A single axis applies to every output, and a list that follows the structure of the output gives each part its own axis.
`NULL` returns an output as it is, which is allowed for an output that does not depend on the arguments mapped over:

```{r}
h <- function(x, w) list(scaled = x * w, total = sum(w))

h_vec <- vectorize(h, in_axes = list(x = -1L), out_axes = list(scaled = 1L, total = NULL))
jit(h_vec)(x, w)
```

## Composing with Other Transformations

`vectorize()` composes with `gradient()` and with itself.
A common use is computing one gradient per observation, e.g. to clip them individually.
The loss below is written for a single observation `x`; vectorizing its gradient over `x` gives the gradient of every observation with respect to the shared parameters `w`:

```{r}
loss <- function(w, x) sum(x * w)^2
per_example_grad <- jit(vectorize(gradient(loss, wrt = "w"), in_axes = list(x = -1L)))

per_example_grad(w, x)
```

Nesting two calls maps over two axes, here forming all pairwise products of two vectors.
The outer call's batch axis comes last, so `a` runs along the columns:

```{r}
outer_product <- vectorize(vectorize(function(a, b) a * b, in_axes = list(b = -1L)), in_axes = list(a = -1L))
jit(outer_product)(nv_array(c(1, 2, 3), dtype = "f32"), nv_array(c(10, 20), dtype = "f32"))
```

## Random Numbers

A function that draws random numbers (see the [random numbers](random-numbers.html) article) draws numbers of its own for every slice.
They are the numbers a loop applying it to one slice after the other draws, and the random state advances as it does after that loop, so vectorizing a simulation changes how fast it runs, not its results:

```{r}
noisy <- function(x) x + nv_runif(shape = 2L)

nv_set_seed(1L)
jit(vectorize(noisy))(x)

nv_set_seed(1L)
noisy_jit <- jit(noisy)
lapply(1:3, function(j) noisy_jit(x[, j]))
```

With `randomness = "same"`, as in PyTorch's `torch.func.vmap()`, every slice draws the same numbers, the ones a single application of the function draws, and the random state advances as after that application:

```{r}
nv_set_seed(1L)
jit(vectorize(noisy, randomness = "same"))(x)
```
